title: Scheduling ISMP 2024
contribution: Describes the three-stage MIP pipeline (clique-based talk groups selected by a set-partitioning MIP, stability-rewarding re-optimization, rank-matching room assignment) used to schedule the 1,265 regular talks of ISMP 2024 in Montréal, and releases anonymized instances to MIPLIB 2024.
problem_entry: Scale of the group's own community conference (~1,600 participants, >1,300 talks) makes manual scheduling impossible; requirements listed in words as four hard constraints, one 'If possible' constraint and soft goals (pp. 3-5).
key_idea: Generate candidate talk groups as cliques of a shared-keyword graph (<=4 talks) and prune streams by keyword mining, then let a MIP choose groups, streams and blocks with affinity bonuses and penalized stream copies; re-optimize with +6/+5 bonuses for staying in the previous slot/day; assign rooms by matching capacity rank to stream-size rank (pp. 5-12).
assumptions: Affinity = shared keywords + preferred streams; groups must be cliques (a strong condition, conceded p. 15); hand-set bonuses (b_suggested 5/3, alpha = 200, b ~ -0.2); U_talk = 4, short blocks {3,6,9,12}; two-stage split with stage-2 feasibility guaranteed by parallel sessions <= |R| (pp. 7-15).
proof_devices: clique necessary condition for promising groups, with the bound sum_{i<=U} C(|I|,i) on candidates and a pair filter (>=2 common keywords) (pp. 5-6)
soft 'same stream not in parallel' constraint modeled by stream copies with weight w(k) = -i for the i-th copy (p. 9)
stability bonus for re-optimization: c(l,k)+6 same stream and block, +5 same stream and day (p. 10)
upstream aggregate constraint (parallel sessions <= |R|) guaranteeing downstream room-assignment feasibility (p. 10)
rank-matching exponential room bonus plus consecutive-triple variables y_{k,p,r} for sessions 'without holes' (pp. 11-12)
experiments: One real instance, Gurobi 11.0.0 on i7-12700 (20 threads): talk assignment 3,000 s, gap 0.2351%, 32,111 rows x 1,927,811 columns, all 198 preferred-stream talks satisfied; rooms 20.89 s, gap 0.0039%; 17 re-optimizations, 3 published, ~47 requests, moved-talk counts reported (sums 1,240/1,251 vs 1,265 unexplained); no baseline comparison (pp. 13-14).
positioning: Minimal: prior ISMP tools (2018 Scheduler; 2012/2015 model in a bachelor's thesis) and six conference-scheduling papers listed in the abstract without comparison (p. 3).
writing: Technical-report register; each constraint glossed in plain words; notation in an appendix; hedging reserved for solution quality, which is 'difficult to quantify' (pp. 7, 12, 14-16).
limits_future: Cliques lose information, hard constraints may leave participants unsatisfied, quality unquantified; future: abstract-similarity metrics, non-clique groups, soft co-authorship constraints, a reusable user interface (p. 15).

method_links.note: Anonymized real ISMP instances with all participant constraints submitted to MIPLIB 2024 (outside DFO).
Classification applied to requirements: hard constraints 1-4, 'if possible' constraint 5 as penalized stream copies, wishes as bonuses.
Heuristic candidate generation + exact MIP selection, but the heuristic restricts what the exact stage can reach (optimal only for the restricted problem), acknowledged by the authors.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Objective bonuses tied to the last published schedule (+6 same slot, +5 same day) and moved-talk counts as the stability metric.
Group schedules its own field's flagship conference and submits the anonymized instance to MIPLIB 2024.

transferable: Write requirements in tiers (hard, 'if possible', objectives) before notation and trace each modeling device to one tier.
Generate set-partitioning columns from a cheap necessary condition (cliques of a similarity graph) and let the MIP choose; state the filter's cost as a limit.
For re-optimization of a published plan, reward staying close to the previous solution in the objective instead of hard-fixing it.
Guarantee feasibility of a later decomposition stage with an aggregate constraint in the earlier stage.
Report instance size (rows, columns, nonzeros), time budget, final gap and, for re-optimizations, how many items moved between published versions.
Submit anonymized instances of a real applied model to the field's standard library (MIPLIB).
coauthors: M. Gervais-Dubé, A. Hertz, S. Le Digabel, A. Legrain

quotes.text: After the initial schedule is published online for participants, it is crucial to minimize the number of changes in subsequent schedules to avoid disrupting their event planning.
Furthermore, only cliques were considered to form group of talks. Since this is a strong condition, some information is lost in the process.

title: Solar: a solar thermal power plant simulator for blackbox optimization benchmarking
contribution: Releases solar, an open-source, platform-reproducible C++ simulator of a molten-salt CSP tower plant parametrized into ten frozen benchmark instances (5-29 mixed/categorical variables, 1-2 objectives, 0-17 a priori/simulation/hidden constraints, stochastic outputs with seeds and replications, variable fidelity), with starting points, best-known values and difficulty diagnostics.
problem_entry: Benchmarking gap: real engineering blackboxes are proprietary, analytic test sets are crucial but unrepresentative, and existing realistic problems each have only some BBO pathologies; entry by listing the pathologies a benchmark must carry (pp. 2-3).
key_idea: One physics simulator from a 2015 MSc thesis, instrumented with switches (instance, seed, rep, fid), anti-triviality constraint models and a material-based cost model, frozen as release 1.0 with instances named solarX.1 and an in-house RNG checked by solar -check (pp. 3, 11-27).
assumptions: Point-source sun, 1 kW/m2, clear day, flat heliostats without tracking errors (may overestimate performance), neglected internal convection, 6 m/s wind, epsilon-NTU or ideal exchanger, steady state, 95% generator efficiency, creep ignored; constraint semantics by the Le Digabel-Wild taxonomy (a priori unrelaxable, simulation QRSK, hidden NUSH) (pp. 8-13, 18-23).
proof_devices: benchmark non-triviality certificate: active bounds and saturated constraints at best-known x* vs x0 (Table 15, pp. 28-29)
feasibility-rate contrast: 10,000 LH points vs a 400n-evaluation NOMAD 3 run, split into a priori, all, hidden (Table 13, p. 24)
coefficient of variation per stochastic output at 100 points x 100 seeds (Fig. 8, p. 25)
fidelity diagnostics: time vs fidelity, constraint-label errors near x*, objective error vs time (Figs. 9-11, pp. 27-29)
local sensitivity: feasibility proportion in balls B_r(x*) for r from 1e-7 to 0.1 (Figs. 14-15, pp. 31-32)
experiments: Budget 400n (150n for solar5.1); LH vs NOMAD 3 feasibility table; replication counts under a Gauss stopping rule on an Apple M2 Max (solar2.1 at x* ~12 days); data profiles on solar6.1 from 30 LH starts for NOMAD 3, NOMAD 4, CMA-ES (none systematically reaches the best known); solar8.1 fronts from several solvers at 5,000 evaluations (pp. 24-30).
positioning: Continues the group's benchmarking line (textbook, applications survey, NOMAD, constraint taxonomy); credits realistic predecessors (groundwater community problems, STYRENE, heat intercepts, Lockwood) and states CSP optimization papers do not provide benchmarking tools; praises analytic test sets before calling them unrepresentative (pp. 2-3).
writing: Hedged then strong novelty claim ('it seems that no work exhibits...' then 'solar is the first realistic blackbox...'); single 'main contribution'; user-manual register in Section 4 with explicit instance recommendations; 'we believe' for difficulty (pp. 3, 21-31).
limits_future: Model simplifications may overestimate performance, creep ignored, bugs may remain (framed as realistic), unbounded variables left to users, x* coordinates withheld; future: new instances and a community results database via nomad@gerad.ca (pp. 8, 13, 17-18, 23, 28, 32).

method_links.note: Thesis model -> standalone executable with fixed I/O, classified constraints, fidelity surrogates, seeds/replications, starting points, credited best-known values, public repo with solver logs.
Variables kept in physical units with some unbounded integers (not scaled to [0,100], step 2); only best-known values released, not x* coordinates (step 5).
A priori/unrelaxable constraints checked before simulation with cnt_eval=false and 1e20 outputs; simulation constraints relaxable (QRSK); hidden constraints as failures; most suggested x0 infeasible.
Budgets in multiples of n, data profiles over 30 starting points, CMA-ES as another-family solver; used to certify difficulty rather than rank solvers.
Starting points in NOMAD syntax, NOMAD logs shipped, results collected at nomad@gerad.ca.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Anti-triviality constraint models by design plus diagnostics (LH vs solver feasibility, CoV, fidelity mislabeling, active constraints at x*, feasibility in balls).
Release 1.0 frozen; instances named solarX.1; bug fixes only in release 2.0; solar -check for platform reproducibility.
Students of the MTH8418 DFO course among the beta-testers who supplied best-known values.

transferable: Open a benchmark paper with the list of real-problem pathologies and a table showing each one present in at least one instance.
Add constraint models whose only job is to make the optimum non-trivial, and replace scale-based descriptive sub-models with ones that respond to design variables.
Freeze a released benchmark and put the major version in the instance name (solarX.1).
Ship an in-house RNG and a self-check command so stochastic outputs are identical across platforms.
Return a sentinel value and a count-evaluation flag so a-priori-rejected points are not charged to the budget.
Certify difficulty with random-sampling vs solver feasibility rates, CoV per output, fidelity-vs-error plots and active constraints at the best-known point.
State each modeling simplification with the direction of the error it introduces.
coauthors: N. Andrés-Thió, M. Diago, A. E. Gheribi, S. Le Digabel, X. Lebeuf, M. Lemyre Garneau, C. Tribes

quotes.text: In fact, it seems that no work exhibits a realistic application specifically developed for BBO benchmarking.
Without them, the solution to many of the problems would be trivial or impractical.

title: A distance for mixed-variable and hierarchical domains with meta variables
contribution: Generalizes the group's single-level meta-variable framework to arbitrary DAG hierarchies (roles meta, meta-decreed, decreed, neutral) and defines a deterministic, constant-time metric (meta distance) on points that do not share variables, via an extended domain with an EXC value and a proven bijection; illustrated with KNN/IDW models on 40 hyperparameter datasets.
problem_entry: Heterogeneous mixed-variable datasets are split into homogeneous subsets, which hurts when data is scarce or expensive; existing distances are random, lack metric axioms (identity of indiscernibles) or cost O(N^3 log N) (pp. 2, 4, 7).
key_idea: Extend every point with its excluded variables set to EXC, organize decree dependencies in a role DAG with universal/restricted sets, define a per-variable included-excluded distance (d, 0, or theta >= sup d/2) aggregated by an l_p norm, and induce it on the original domain through the bijective transfer mapping (pp. 8-20).
assumptions: Role graph is a DAG (Assumption 1, justified by a two-variable circular example); theta >= sup d/2; bounded restricted sets (else theta = infinity); p >= 1; any 1D distance in the both-included case (pp. 11, 17-19).
proof_devices: minimal contradiction example (two circular meta-decreed binaries) placed before the DAG assumption (p. 11)
bijection proof by deleting EXC nodes from the role graph (Thm. 2, pp. 15-16)
case analysis on EXC patterns for the triangle inequality, where only the case u,v included and z excluded needs theta >= sup d/2 (Thm. 3, pp. 17-18)
reindexing per-variable distances into one vector and identifying the meta distance with its l_p norm (Thm. 4, p. 19)
extend-then-induce: define the metric on an extended domain and transfer it through a bijection (Cor. 1, p. 20)
experiments: 40 datasets (5 variants x 4 sizes x MLP/Fashion-MNIST or CNN/CIFAR10); KNN classification with 20 seeds where Hybrid is best overall and Meta best only on variant #1; IDW regression tuned by NOMAD (200 n evaluations, 33% LHS, 200 instances) with data profiles at tau = 10%, 2.5%, 0.5% on validation and test RMSE, Meta best; data-aggregation curves mixed on CNN (pp. 20-25, 28-29).
positioning: Two comparison tables (vs graph distances; feature matrix vs subproblems, own prior framework, variable-size kernel, Hutter-Osborne kernel, EMI); mechanism-based criticism (pseudo-distances without identity of indiscernibles, O(N^3 log N) cost); claims to generalize tree-structured, variable-size, conditional/NAS and hierarchical spaces (pp. 3-7, 25).
writing: 'This work has two main contributions' early; one running MLP example through five figures; numbered comments after definitions; Corollary 1 followed by a four-step recap; hedged discussion ('should provide', 'seems to confirm') (pp. 2-25).
limits_future: theta must be infinite for unbounded sets, scaling of categorical/excluded variables ambiguous, only simple models tested; future: incompatibilities between values (in progress), Gaussian processes and Bayesian optimization, broader experiments (pp. 19-20, 27).

method_links.note: Semantics-first applied to inputs: every variable gets a type and a role in a role DAG before the model or distance is chosen.
DAG hypothesis justified by a minimal contradiction; theta bound is exactly what the triangle inequality needs, with its cost stated; no guarantee ladder.
Data profiles in groups of (n+1) evaluations at three tolerances with seeds; losses of the proposed method reported.
Model parameters tuned by NOMAD (MADS) as a blackbox with LHS start (also Heuristic 7).
Scripts and data released at github.com/bbopt/graph_distance (weak).

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: generalize your own framework, shown in a feature table
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Own 2023 meta framework listed as a row of Table 2 with its gaps; paper generalizes it to arbitrary hierarchy levels and adds a distance.
Extended points with EXC, bijective transfer mapping, metric on the extended domain, induced metric on the original domain.

transferable: State the research gap as a short list of defects each existing method has at least one of, then tabulate methods against those defects.

To compare objects that do not share coordinates, extend them to a common coordinate set with a sentinel value, give a per-coordinate rule for sentinel pairs, prove the extension is a bijection and induce the metric back.
Put the smallest breaking example right before a structural assumption (acyclicity).
Isolate the one case of a triangle-inequality proof that forces a parameter bound and make that bound the hypothesis.

coauthors: E. Hallé-Hannan, Y. Diouane, S. Le Digabel, P. Saves

quotes.text: This is problematic, particularly in optimization, as distinct points with a distance of zero can lead to convergence issues or unreliable exploration.
Heterogeneous datasets are often partitioned into homogeneous data subsets of similar types that are easier to tackle: this approach is undesirable when data is limited or expensive-to-generate

title: Benchmarking constrained, multi-objective and surrogate-assisted derivative-free optimization methods
contribution: Reviews convergence plots and accuracy, performance and data profiles for DFO and formally extends them to infeasible starting points, multi-objective problems (normalized hypervolume accuracy) and surrogate-assisted methods (weighted effort N = N_t + w N_s), implemented in the open-source RunnerPost tool.
problem_entry: Existing benchmarking tools silently assume easy feasibility, a single objective and no surrogate; in DFO the effort is simulation calls, so each hidden assumption breaks one quantity (pp. 3-4, 10).
key_idea: Keep tau-solve and the profile definitions, but redefine the baseline f0 (first feasible values across algorithms), the quality measure (hypervolume within an ideal-nadir box from the union of fronts) and the effort count (weighted surrogate evaluations, time, or Monte Carlo repetitions), under setup rules for test sets, algorithm sets and logs (pp. 4-15).
assumptions: Evaluation dominates algorithm cost; comparable stopping criteria and logged evaluation number, objective and feasibility flag; same initial points for all algorithms; w equals the true relative cost; (n_p+1) scaling from simplex gradients (pp. 4-5, 9, 13, 15).
proof_devices: digits-of-accuracy equivalence -log10(1 - f_acc) >= d <=> f_acc >= 1 - 10^-d (p. 7)
tau-solve rewritten as f(x) <= f* + tau (f0 - f*) (p. 8)
switching phenomenon shown by re-plotting performance profiles without the best algorithm (ratio range 40 -> 12) (pp. 9, 13-14)
two-panel convergence plot: violation h until first feasible point eta_a, then best feasible f (p. 11)
closed-form 2D hypervolume as a sum of rectangles (p. 13)
experiments: None on real problems; illustrative anonymized data designed to exhibit pitfalls (evaluations vs time, ranking reversal with tau, f0 choice, w = 0 vs 1/10), all plots generated by RunnerPost (pp. 4, 6-16).
positioning: Builds on Dolan-Moré, Moré-Wild, Beiranvand-Hare-Lucet (accuracy profiles), Gould-Scott (switching), filter methods and the group's indicator review without criticizing anyone (pp. 4, 7-12).
writing: Tutorial, prescriptive register ('should', 'It is recommended'); each profile given with definition, axis ranges, monotonicity and a numeric reading of an example figure; discussion restates three extensions and ends with a hope sentence (pp. 5-16).
limits_future: No limitations section; future only combining techniques (multi-objective surrogate-based); discussion claims hidden-constraint handling that the body reduces to inf/NaN log flags (pp. 5, 16).

method_links.note: Evaluation count as currency, data profiles in groups of n+1, several tau, accuracy profiles described as not considering effort.
Small representative test set preferred to large unrelated one; derivative-based algorithms excluded and algorithm set kept very low, narrowing 'another family' to DFO families.
Constrained benchmarking needs eta_a, violation h and a feasible-only baseline; logs separate failed evaluations.
The instrument is a post-processing tool (RunnerPost, MIT) rather than the solver; every plot comes from it.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Same f0 and f* for all algorithms, f0 from first feasible points under infeasible starts (min or max, both shown), drop and flag instances nobody improves.
N = N_t + w N_s with w the relative cost; several weights for several surrogates; repetitions for Monte Carlo fidelity.

transferable: Log at least evaluation number, objective value and a feasibility flag, with inf/NaN for failed evaluations.
Fix f0 and f* identically for all algorithms; remove and flag instances that no algorithm improves.

For infeasible starts, plot the violation h until the first feasible point and the best feasible f afterwards, and show that the f0 choice (min or max of first feasible values) does not change the conclusion.
Count surrogate-assisted effort as N = N_t + w N_s with w the measured cost ratio, and show profiles at w = 0 and at the realistic w.
Show the dependence of performance profiles on the algorithm set by re-plotting without the best solver.
For each plot type introduced, give axis ranges, monotonicity and one sentence reading numbers off an example figure.

It is recommended to keep the number of algorithms very low.
